title: Maximum Spending After Buying Items
statement:
There are `m` shops with `n` items each, and `values[i][j]` is the value of item `j` in shop `i`. Every row of `values` is ordered from largest to smallest (`values[i][j] >= values[i][j + 1]`).

You buy exactly one item per day, on days `d = 1, 2, 3, ...`, until all `m * n` items are bought. On day `d` you may choose any shop that still has items left, but from that shop you must take the not-yet-bought item with the **largest index** `j`, and it costs `values[i][j] * d`. Items of different shops are separate goods, even when they share an index.

Return the largest total amount of money you can spend on buying everything.
constraints: Each values[i] is sorted in non-increasing order
notes:
## Intuition

Later days multiply prices by bigger numbers, so to spend the most you want the cheapest items early and the most valuable ones late; by the rearrangement inequality, buying all items in increasing order of value is the best any order can do. The shop rule never gets in the way: because each row is sorted from largest to smallest, the item a shop offers next (its rightmost one) is always that shop's cheapest remaining item. So on each day, buying the cheapest of the offered items follows the global increasing order exactly. Trying every buying order would also work but explodes combinatorially.

## Approach

1. Keep `next[shop]`, the index of the item each shop offers now, starting at `n - 1`.
2. For each `day` from 1 to `m * n`, scan the shops that still have items and pick `best`, the one offering the smallest value.
3. Add that value times `day` to `total`, and move that shop's pointer one item left.
4. After the last day, return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

The shops first offer `2, 1, 3`. Day 1 buys `1` (shop 1), day 2 buys `2` (shop 0), day 3 buys `3` (shop 2), then `4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9` on days 4 to 9. That is `1·1 + 2·2 + ... + 9·9 = 285`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n · m): each of the `m · n` days scans at most `m` shops (m ≤ 10). A heap would make it O(m · n · log m).
- Space: O(m) for the pointers.

## Pitfalls

- Skip shops whose pointer has gone below 0; they have nothing left to sell.
- Buying the most valuable item first gives the smallest spending, the opposite of what is asked.
- On LeetCode the total reaches about 5 · 10^15, and `value * day` overflows a 32-bit int, so Java and C must multiply in 64 bits.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `next[shop]` | index of the item that shop offers next (-1 when empty) |
| `day` | the current day, also the price multiplier |
| `best` | shop with the cheapest offered item today |
| `total` | money spent so far |

narration.4: Every shop starts by offering its last, cheapest item.
narration.6: Buy exactly one item on each of the m * n days.
narration.7: No shop chosen yet for this day.
narration.8: Look at what every shop offers today.
narration.9: A shop whose pointer passed the front is sold out.
narration.10: Keep the shop whose offered item is the cheapest so far.
narration.14: Pay the chosen item's value times the day number.
narration.15: That shop now offers the next item to the left.
narration.17: All items are bought; return the money spent.
